drills.q: State the trait bound difference between arguments 1..15 and argument 16 of an axum handler, and name the hard arity cap.
drills.a: Arguments 1..15 are bound by `FromRequestParts<S>` (takes `&mut http::request::Parts`, head only). The last argument is bound by `FromRequest<S>` (takes `Request` by value, consuming the body). The cap is 16, generated by `all_the_tuples!` in axum-core; a 17th argument fails the `Handler` bound with an opaque error.

drills.q: Recite the sqlx `PoolOptions::new()` defaults for max_connections, acquire_timeout, idle_timeout, max_lifetime, and test_before_acquire.
drills.a: max_connections = 10, acquire_timeout = 30 s, idle_timeout = 600 s (10 min), max_lifetime = 1800 s (30 min), test_before_acquire = true. Also min_connections = 0, acquire_slow_threshold = 2 s, fair = true, statement cache capacity 100.

drills.q: What is axum's `DefaultBodyLimit`, and which extractors does it apply to?
drills.a: 2 MB. It applies to `Bytes` and everything built on it: `String`, `Json`, `Form`. It does NOT apply to an extractor that consumes the body directly via `Body::poll_frame`. Override per-route with `DefaultBodyLimit::max(n)` or globally with `tower_http::limit::RequestBodyLimitLayer`.

drills.q: Given `ServiceBuilder::new().layer(A).layer(B).service(router)` and `router.layer(A).layer(B)`, which layer sees the request first in each?
drills.a: ServiceBuilder: A first (it builds A(B(router)); tower's docs say layers added first are called with the request first). Chained Router::layer: B first (it builds B(A(router)), because each `layer` call wraps whatever the router currently is). The two read identically and mean the opposite, which is why the convention is one ServiceBuilder passed to one `.layer()` call.

drills.q: A service serves 2,000 rps, each request holds a connection for 3 ms, and runs 10 replicas with maxSurge 2 against a default Postgres. Size the pool and show the arithmetic.
drills.a: Little's Law: L = 2000 x 0.003 = 6 mean connections. Target utilisation 0.7 (queueing delay grows as 1/(1-rho)), so ~9. But the constraint is the database: (10 + 2) x pool <= 100 - 3 reserved, so pool <= 8. Take 8 per replica. If you need more, add PgBouncer in transaction mode rather than raising Postgres max_connections, and set acquire_timeout to ~3 s so exhaustion is a fast 503.

drills.q: An endpoint returns 200 with no auth token. `.layer(RequireAuth)` is present in the code. Name the two most likely causes.
drills.a: (1) `.layer()` was called before the `.route()` that declares the endpoint; `Router::layer` only wraps routes that already exist, so it wrapped nothing. (2) The route lives in a sub-`Router` that was `merge`d in after the layer was applied. Fix: all routes first, layer last; use `route_layer` for auth so 404s do not become 401s; add an integration test that hits every route unauthenticated over HTTP.

drills.q: Your `count(*)` came back typed `Option<i64>` from `sqlx::query!`. Explain and fix.
drills.a: Postgres reports nullability conservatively for aggregates, expressions, and columns on the nullable side of a LEFT JOIN, so sqlx types them as `Option<T>`. Fix with the column annotation: `count(o.id) as "order_count!: i64"`, where `!` forces non-null, `?` forces nullable, and `: Type` overrides the Rust type. Note sqlx 0.9.0 changed Postgres nullability inference (breaking), so this can shift on upgrade.

drills.q: Traces show unrelated requests nested under each other, only in production under load. Diagnose in one sentence and give the fix.
drills.a: Someone held a `span.enter()` guard across an `.await`; `Span::enter()` sets a thread-local current span, so when the task yields the worker polls a different task whose events are attributed to the entered span. Fix: `#[tracing::instrument]` or `.instrument(span)`, which enter and exit around each individual poll.

drills.q: Write the four-stage cargo-chef Dockerfile skeleton and say which layer is the cached one.
drills.a: chef base (`lukemathwalker/cargo-chef:latest-rust-<ver>`); planner (`COPY . .` then `cargo chef prepare --recipe-path recipe.json`); builder (`COPY --from=planner recipe.json`, then `cargo chef cook --release --recipe-path recipe.json`, then `COPY . .` and `cargo build --release`); runtime (`FROM gcr.io/distroless/cc-debian12:nonroot`, COPY the binary). The cached layer is `cargo chef cook`, invalidated only by Cargo.toml/Cargo.lock. Measured: cold 117 s, warm 24 s, 4.9x.

drills.q: Throughput scales fine to 2 threads and flattens at 8; only in the Alpine image; `perf` shows time in `malloc`. Root cause and two fixes.
drills.a: musl's allocator serialises multithreaded allocation far harder than glibc's ptmalloc, and Rust allocates on every String/Vec/boxed future; reported slowdowns reach 7x and worsen with thread count. Fix 1 (preferred): build for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and run on distroless/cc-debian12. Fix 2 (if a static binary is mandatory): `#[global_allocator]` set to mimalloc or tikv-jemallocator.

drills.q: Every pod restarts within 30 seconds of a brief database slowdown, and the database then falls over. Walk the causal chain and the fix.
drills.a: The liveness probe queries the database. Kubernetes defaults are periodSeconds 10 / timeoutSeconds 1 / failureThreshold 3, so 30 s after the first failed probe every pod is SIGKILLed simultaneously; they all restart and reconnect at once, so the database gets a connection storm from every replica and stays down. Fix: liveness checks the process only; move the DB check to readiness (which removes traffic without killing the pod); add a startupProbe; cap acquire_timeout so pool waits do not stall the probe.

drills.q: Design the shutdown path so a rolling deploy produces zero 502s and no lost work.
drills.a: preStop `sleep 5` so Endpoints propagate before you stop accepting (SIGTERM and Endpoints removal are concurrent; kube-proxy converges in 1-5 s). `axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(signal)` to drain in-flight requests, wrapped in a `tokio::time::timeout(25s)` so a long-poll cannot outlast terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s). Then `pool.close().await` and shut down the tracer provider so the last span batch flushes. Detached `tokio::spawn`ed work is NOT drained by graceful shutdown: use a CancellationToken plus TaskTracker or an mpsc you drain.

drills.q: Pods die with exit code 137 and no logs. Rust has no GC, so where did the memory go, and what do you check?
drills.a: There is no `OutOfMemoryError`; the kernel SIGKILLs on the cgroup limit, so you get no stack, no log, no flushed spans. Check: unbounded request bodies (DefaultBodyLimit is 2 MB but streaming extractors bypass it, so add RequestBodyLimitLayer), unbounded channels, and glibc arena growth (ptmalloc creates up to 8 x ncores arenas retaining freed memory, which looks like a leak; set MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2 or switch to jemalloc/mimalloc). Alert on container_memory_working_set_bytes vs the limit rather than waiting for the restart.

drills.q: Argue against building a new internal CRUD service in Rust. Give four concrete conditions.
drills.a: (1) The bottleneck is not the service: at 200 rps with 95% of time waiting on Postgres, axum/FastAPI/Spring Boot have the same p99 within noise. (2) The shape changes weekly: in discovery, every schema change means `cargo sqlx prepare` plus a wave of type errors, which is a feature in year three and a tax in month two. (3) Staffing: the hiring pool is an order of magnitude smaller and ramp is 2-3 months for async Rust. (4) Ecosystem gaps that matter to you: Kafka client, AWS SDK, and OpenTelemetry traces (still Beta at the 0.32 line while Logs and Metrics are Stable). The honest case for Rust is operational, not benchmark: 8 replicas instead of 40, no GC saw-tooth in p99, a 26 MB image with a dozen packages of CVE surface.

drills.q: You set `panic = "abort"` and added `CatchPanicLayer`. What actually happens when a handler panics, and why?
drills.a: The whole process dies, taking every in-flight request with it. `CatchPanicLayer` is built on `std::panic::catch_unwind`, which is a no-op under `panic = "abort"` because there are no unwind tables; Tokio's per-task panic isolation (`JoinError::is_panic`) is gone for the same reason. On a service, keep the default `panic = "unwind"`, add `CatchPanicLayer` inside the trace layer so the span still closes, and set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`.
